nm_cave_main_area.blurb: The main cave of La Bajada Canyon, on the southern rim of the Caja del Rio plateau outside Santa Fe. It is a huge, steep amphitheater of overhanging basalt, and the lines are long and powerful sport climbs, many needing a 70 m rope, with fixed draws common. Nearly everything is 5.11 or harder, with most of the climbs at 5.12 and 5.13, so it suits strong climbers. The rock can be glassy or loose and some routes start in a crumbly band, so wear a helmet. The deep overhang keeps it mostly shaded in summer and sunny in winter. The setting is remote and usually quiet.
nm_cave_main_area.parking_note: Reached by dirt roads from the La Cienega side, crossing public land for several miles before a two-track leads to a small pull-out where a trail starts. Ground clearance helps, and the roads turn to mud after rain. From the trail end, a steep descent drops into the canyon and the cave.

nm_major_wall.blurb: A sport wall in the southern part of the Box, a rhyolite canyon southwest of Socorro. The rock here is volcanic and mostly solid, though quality varies across the canyon. Climbing is mainly bolted lines with a few trad routes, spread across a wide range of difficulty from easy 5.5 up through the low 5.14s, with a decent block of climbs in the 5.9 to 5.13 range. The harder lines are the headline attractions. A good trail leads to the wall from the south parking area. Winter days are pleasant here, while summer can be hot and buggy, so mornings are the better choice then.
nm_major_wall.parking_note: Drive into the Box off the highway southwest of Socorro and continue to the southern parking, roughly a mile beyond the main northern lot. Avoid the turnaround and stay on the established trail from the lot's north end.

nm_north_west_side.blurb: The north and west faces of the Overlook, a basalt crag on the rim of White Rock Canyon above the Rio Grande. The cliff is an L-shaped wall, around 65 feet tall, and is known as White Rock's best sport crag. Most climbs here are bolted with anchors, with some gear-protected cracks and a few top-rope lines. Grades run from the 5.8s into the 5.12s, with plenty in the 5.11 and 5.12 range. Because the cliff turns in several directions, there is usually a side in sun or shade, and this side is the cooler one on warm days.
nm_north_west_side.parking_note: Follow the main road through White Rock, turn onto Rover Boulevard, then Meadow Lane, and go left into Overlook Park. Leave the car by the roundabout at the road's end near the viewpoint.
nm_north_west_side.approach: From the viewpoint, follow the rim trail along a narrow ridge to the top of the cliff, then scramble down to the anchor level. A climber's trail winds down to the base.

nm_solar_cave_2.blurb: An overhanging cave in Diablo Canyon, above the Rio Grande near Santa Fe, and the home of some of the canyon's hardest sport climbing. The basalt looks crumbly in places but is quite solid. Nearly all of the climbs are bolted, with most around 5.12 and 5.13 and only a handful in the 5.10s and 5.11s, so it is a destination for strong, steep-rock climbers. The cave takes plenty of sun and is exposed in the afternoon, which makes it a better winter or cool-weather choice. Rockfall is a concern in the canyon, so wear a helmet.
nm_solar_cave_2.parking_note: Drive Old Buckman Road west out of Santa Fe and follow the washboard dirt road to the trailhead area at the canyon's edge. The road is rough and can be impassable in bad weather.
nm_solar_cave_2.approach: Walk down into the sandy wash and head up the canyon between the cliffs. Before the walls pinch in, a trail on the right climbs up to the cave.

ny_chapel_pond.blurb: One of the busiest winter climbing venues in the Adirondacks, right beside the road in the Keene Valley. The ice forms early, and the routes sit on a northeast-facing wall that catches a little morning sun and then stays shaded. The climbing is mostly water ice with a smaller share of mixed lines. Most of the ice is moderate, with a lot of WI3 and WI4, plus some harder WI5 and WI6 for stronger parties. Mixed routes range from about M4 to M7. Weekends bring crowds, so start early to get a line.
ny_chapel_pond.parking_note: The lot sits beside the road right at the pond. When it is full, cars can pull off along either shoulder nearby.
ny_chapel_pond.approach: Very short. The pond and the nearest ice are a stone's throw from the parking area, and the canyon routes are reached across the frozen water.

ny_d_harvest_moon_to_the_end.blurb: The far, southern stretch of the Near Trapps, the second most visited cliff in the Gunks. The routes here are almost all traditional climbs on horizontal-cracked conglomerate, with a spread of grades from the easiest 5th class up into the 5.12s, and most falling between 5.6 and 5.11. A bold hand-size crack splitting the White Pillar's right flank marks the break in the cliff here. The better climbing is out at the far end, away from the dense, popular stretch near the road. Protection is often sporty, and grades are stiff, so expect to feel the numbers.
ny_d_harvest_moon_to_the_end.parking_note: Use the lot up the hill past the hairpin turn and the steel bridge. Cross the road with care and take the foot trail south to the base of the cliff, then continue along the cliff to this far end.
ny_d_harvest_moon_to_the_end.approach: Plan on a longer walk than at the north end of the cliff, along the base trail beneath the routes. The middle section has loose rock, so watch for falling debris.

ny_a2_the_uberfall_right.blurb: The first stretch of rock you meet walking north from the steel bridge at the Trapps, and a very social spot on busy days. The cliff is quartz conglomerate with horizontal cracks, and the climbing is mostly traditional with a few top-rope lines. Grades go from easy fifth class to the low 5.12s, with a good number of moderates and a cluster in the 5.10s and 5.11s. Most routes begin right by the carriage road, and many have bolted anchors, while others need a walk-off. Spring and fall weekends are crowded, and the prime season is autumn.
ny_a2_the_uberfall_right.approach: Short. The carriage road runs along the foot of the cliff, and the routes start a few steps from it.

ny_b_jackie_and_friends.blurb: A section of the Trapps lying between the Uberfall toilet and the big left-facing chimney of Miss Bailey. The rock is Gunks conglomerate, with the horizontal cracks, roofs and jugs the area is known for, and the routes are almost all traditional, with a few top-rope lines. Grades span from 5.2 up to 5.12, with a fairly even spread from the moderates through the 5.10s and 5.11s. It is easy to reach from the carriage road. In summer the foliage hides the cliff, so newcomers can have trouble finding their route, and weekends in spring and fall are busy.
ny_b_jackie_and_friends.approach: A short walk from the carriage road along the base; the yellow-marked access trails reach the wall in a few minutes.

ny_millbrook.blurb: The remote end of the Gunks, a tall cliff of around 350 feet on the southern end of the ridge, reached by a long walk on trails and used more by regulars than by first-time visitors. The climbing is traditional and adventurous, with a few aid lines, and it is steeper and harder than the busier cliffs. Most routes fall in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with 5.12 the single biggest group. Big boulders sit at the base. Expect a quiet day, a serious approach and rockfall care, and bring a full rack. Fall is the prime season.
ny_millbrook.approach: Roughly an hour of rambling trail walking from the main cliff parking areas to reach the cliff.

ny_e_the_mac_wall.blurb: A stretch of the Trapps that runs from Three Pines across to the big orange right-facing corner of Asphodel. The rock is quartz conglomerate with the horizontal cracks, roofs and jugs that define Gunks climbing, and nearly everything is a traditional route, with a couple of top-rope lines. It leans toward the harder side of the cliff: the biggest group is at 5.10, with plenty of 5.11 and some 5.12 and 5.13 for good measure, and only a handful of moderates. Protection is often sporty and grades run stiff. The cliff is hidden by foliage in summer and crowded on spring and fall weekends.
ny_e_the_mac_wall.approach: Short. The carriage road follows the base of the cliff and the access trails reach the wall in a few minutes.
